subject: philosophy
title: What is philosophy?
objective: Turn a familiar conviction into a question worth investigating.

lesson.opening: Philosophical inquiry examines basic questions about reality, knowledge, value, and how to live. These questions have been pursued in many languages and communities. The opening route uses transferable reasoning tools before a focused study of Socrates; it is not a claim that philosophy began with, or belongs to, Greece.

sections.heading: Inquiry, reasons, and intellectual independence
sections.body:
Suppose two people disagree about a promise. One says it must be kept because a promise creates an obligation. Another says that preventing serious harm matters more. Counting how many people favor each answer will not by itself settle what ought to be done. We need to identify what each person takes to be a reason and ask whether that reason survives difficult cases.

Philosophy is not just having an opinion on a large topic. A useful beginning is to formulate a question clearly, distinguish possible answers, and examine the reasons for them. Some questions concern what exists (metaphysics); some concern what knowledge requires (epistemology); others concern how we should act (ethics). These areas overlap: a claim about what a person is may affect what we think we owe that person.

Understanding and endorsement are different achievements. You can explain why someone thinks promises bind us without agreeing that they bind us without exception. First reconstruct the strongest reasonable version of a claim. Then identify where your disagreement lies. Otherwise you risk answering an easier argument that no one actually offered.

Not every dispute has a quick decisive test. That does not make every answer equally supported. Clarifying a term, finding an inconsistency, or showing that an objection misses its target can be real progress even when the larger question remains open. In this app, correct answers concern reasoning and interpretation—not which ultimate outlook you adopt.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: Mara begins with a claim about reasons. Ilan tests its possible scope with a difficult case. Mara revises the formulation rather than abandoning all obligations. Notice that neither popularity nor force of feeling appears as a premise.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: An objection to this approach says that relentless questioning can prevent action. A serious reply must explain when inquiry should pause for a decision; merely celebrating doubt does not answer the practical problem.

choices: She distinguishes a reason from a reason that overrides every other consideration.
She proves Ilan is always right.

activities.prompt: Which response demonstrates understanding before criticism?
choices: You treat promising as generating an obligation; I question whether that obligation is exceptionless.

activities.prompt: A city must choose a policy tomorrow. Which is the most defensible philosophical next step?
choices: Identify the relevant values, evidence, and tradeoffs, then decide with stated uncertainty.
Treat the loudest view as true.

activities.prompt: Which objection directly addresses unlimited inquiry?
choices: Decisions sometimes must be made before inquiry is complete.

activities.prompt: Which is primarily an epistemological question?
choices: What makes testimony a good reason for belief?

activities.prompt: Two incompatible positions are both carefully studied. What follows?
choices: Studying a position does not settle whether it is true.

activities.prompt: Name one belief you hold. Explain what understanding an opposing argument would require before you criticize it.
activities.context:
Mara: A promise creates a reason to do what you said you would do.
Ilan: Suppose keeping it would expose someone to serious harm. Is that reason always decisive?
Mara: Perhaps not. I need to distinguish having a reason from having an overriding reason.
rubric: I give a fair opposing reason, not a caricature.
I distinguish understanding that reason from agreeing with it.
